name: Bennetland
text: Your train passes near the hamlet of Bennetland, on the train's {side}, which sits between the line to Selby and the line to Doncaster. Its name, first recorded in 1234, is thought to mean a stretch of land overgrown with bent grass.

name: St Michael's Church, Eastrington
text: Your train passes near St Michael's Church, Eastrington, on the train's {side}, built around 1100; parts of its nave and chancel survive from then. The chancel partly collapsed in 1632 and was rebuilt the same year, and the porch has a Norman frieze carved with animals.

name: Wressle Castle
text: Your train passes near Wressle Castle, on the train's {side}, a palace-fortress built for Thomas Percy in the 1390s. It was meant as a grand home rather than a fortress and was never besieged; Parliament held it in the Civil War, and only its south range still stands.

name: Cochrane Shipbuilders
text: Your train passes near the site of Cochrane Shipbuilders' yard, on the train's {side}, which moved here from Beverley in 1898. The River Ouse is so narrow at Selby that the yard launched its ships sideways into the river; it closed in 1992.

name: Bishopsbarns
text: Your train passes near Bishopsbarns, on the train's {side}, the Tudor Revival house that the architect Walter Brierley designed as his own home, finished in 1905, with a garden by Gertrude Jekyll. Its name comes from the barns of the See of York that once stood on the site.

name: Kirkham Priory
text: Your train passes near the ruins of Kirkham Priory, on the train's {side}, on the banks of the River Derwent. The Augustinian priory was founded in the 1120s by Walter l'Espec, who also built Rievaulx Abbey; later the area was used to test D-Day landing vehicles, and Winston Churchill came to visit.

name: Malton Priory
text: Your train passes near Malton Priory, on the train's {side}, founded around 1150 by Eustace fitz John for the Gilbertine Order. Its church is now a parish church, and the only church of the Gilbertine Order still in regular use.

name: Church of St Oswald, Filey
text: Your train passes near the Church of St Oswald, Filey, on the train's {side}, which Pevsner called "easily the finest church in the north-east corner of the East Riding". Its Norman tower was a landmark for sailors between the Tyne and London; the church stands on the north side of a ravine and was in the North Riding, while the rest of the town was in the East Riding.

name: Scarborough Mere
text: Your train passes near Scarborough Mere, on the train's {side}, a natural lake that the railway from York cut in two when it was built in 1845. In the 20th century holidaymakers could sail on a little Spanish galleon, the Hispaniola, to Treasure Island to dig for doubloons.

name: Hunmanby lock-up
text: Your train passes near the Hunmanby lock-up, on the train's {side}, a little brick building with no windows put up in 1834 to hold people for a short while. Inside are two cells, so that two people who had been fighting could be kept apart.

name: Buckton Hall
text: Your train passes near Buckton Hall, on the train's {side}, a chalk-built house of 1744 in the style of John Vanbrugh, on the site of a manor house first recorded in the 13th century. Local legend says tunnels from its cellars to the beach were used by smugglers.

name: Bridlington Spa
text: Your train passes near Bridlington Spa, on the train's {side}, a dance hall, theatre and conference centre looking out over the South Bay. The first Spa opened in 1896; fires in 1906 and 1932 destroyed much of it, but the opera house of 1907 is still part of the building.

name: RAF Carnaby
text: Your train passes near the site of RAF Carnaby, on the train's {side}, an emergency landing strip opened in 1944 for damaged bombers coming home over the coast. Its single runway was five times the width of a standard one, so that crippled aircraft could land more easily.

name: Mortimer's Warehouse
text: Your train passes near Mortimer's Warehouse, on the train's {side}, one of the warehouses built at the head of the Driffield Navigation, the canal that linked the town with the River Hull from 1770. From the 1870s it was the granary of the Mortimers' grain and seed business.

name: Riverhead Court
text: Your train passes near Riverhead Court, on the train's {side}, a large granary built at the head of the Driffield Navigation before the end of the 18th century. It fell out of use in the 20th century and in 1974 was turned into 22 flats.

name: Watton Priory
text: Your train passes near Watton Priory, on the train's {side}, a double monastery of the Gilbertine Order founded in 1150 by Eustace fitz John and his wife Agnes. It was built where an Anglo-Saxon nunnery mentioned by Bede had once stood.

name: Beverley Minster
text: Your train passes near Beverley Minster, on the train's {side}, one of the largest parish churches in the country, bigger than a third of England's cathedrals. Saint John of Beverley, Bishop of York in the early eighth century, founded a monastery here, and his remains lie in a vault beneath the nave.

name: Beverley Friary
text: Your train passes Beverley Friary, on the train's {side}, whose core is a guest house that the Dominican friars added to their priory in the early 14th century. Since 1984 it has been a youth hostel.

name: The Boulevard
text: Your train passes near the site of the Boulevard, on the train's {side}, Hull FC's rugby league ground from 1895 to 2010. Its main entrance on Airlie Street gave the club its nickname, the Airlie Birds, and its liveliest stand was named the Threepenny Stand after its first price of entry.

name: Hessle Whiting Mill
text: Your train passes near Hessle Whiting Mill, on the train's {side}, a tower windmill by the Humber built between 1810 and 1815 to crush chalk into whiting, used in paint. Its sails came off in 1925, but it carried on working with gas and then electric power until the 1950s.

name: Brough Aerodrome
text: Your train passes near the site of Brough Aerodrome, on the train's {side}, first used by the Blackburn Aeroplane & Motor Company in 1916 to test seaplanes. Blackburn built the Beverley transport aircraft and the Buccaneer strike aircraft here; the airfield closed in 2013.

name: Petuaria
text: Your train passes near the site of Petuaria, on the train's {side}, a Roman fort founded in AD 70 where Brough now stands. The town that grew up beside it, with its ferry and port, lasted until about 370 and was probably the capital of the Parisi tribe.

name: Gilberdyke
text: Your train passes near Gilberdyke, on the train's {side}, a village recorded simply as "Dyc" in 1234 and as "Gilberdyke" from 1349. Who the Gilbert in its name was is not known.

name: Hull Truck Theatre
text: Your train passes near Hull Truck Theatre, on the train's {side}. The company was founded in 1971 by the actor and musician Mike Bradwell when he couldn't find work, with an advertisement in Time Out that read "Half-formed theatre company seeks other half".

name: MKM Stadium
text: Your train passes near the MKM Stadium, on the train's {side}, home to both Hull City football club and Hull FC rugby league club. It was finished in 2002 for about £44 million and is owned by Hull City Council; it was first called the KC Stadium.

name: Stainforth and Keadby Canal
text: Your train passes beside the Stainforth and Keadby Canal, on the train's {side}, opened in 1802 to link the River Don Navigation with the River Trent. Richard Dunston's boatyard at Thorne built boats on it from 1858 to 1984; its largest ship needed a dam across the canal, in case it got stuck in Keadby Lock.

name: Keadby Power Stations
text: Your train passes near Keadby Power Stations, on the train's {side}, a pair of gas-fired power stations by the River Trent, built on the site of an older coal-fired one. The first of them began generating in 1996 and uses water from the Trent to condense its steam.

name: Keadby Bridge
text: Your train crosses the River Trent on Keadby Bridge, the King George V Bridge, built by the Great Central Railway between 1912 and 1916 to carry both the railway and a road. Its electrically powered lifting span was one of the first of its kind in Britain and, when built, the largest in Europe.

name: Thornholme Priory
text: Your train passes near the site of Thornholme Priory, on the train's {side}, an Augustinian priory founded in the reign of King Stephen, on the edge of the Ancholme carrs between Broughton and Appleby. It lasted until 1536, when the monasteries were dissolved.

name: Newsham Abbey
text: Your train passes near the site of Newsham Abbey, on the train's {side}, founded in 1143 by Peter of Gousla as a daughter house of an abbey near Calais. It was the first house of the Premonstratensian canons, the White Canons, in England.

name: Newsham Bridge
text: Your train passes near Newsham Bridge, on the train's {side}, a Gothic Revival bridge in Brocklesby Park built around 1772, probably by Capability Brown, over Newsham Lake. Many of its carvings are broken, and it is on the Heritage at Risk Register.

name: St Peter and St Paul's Church, Stallingborough
text: Your train passes near St Peter and St Paul's Church, Stallingborough, on the train's {side}, built of brick from 1779 to 1781 after the medieval church collapsed in 1746. A medieval cross still stands in the churchyard.

name: Stallingborough
text: Your train passes near Stallingborough, on the train's {side}, a village recorded as "Stalinburg" in the Domesday Book. A medieval list of the resting places of saints names it as the burial place of the Anglo-Saxon Saint Avbur.

name: John Whitgift Academy
text: Your train passes near John Whitgift Academy, on the train's {side}, a secondary school named after John Whitgift, who was born in Grimsby and was Archbishop of Canterbury from 1583 to 1604.

name: Grimsby Minster
text: Your train passes Grimsby Minster, on the train's {side}, the church of St James. A church here was handed to Robert Bloet, Bishop of Lincoln, in 1114; its central tower was added in 1365, and it became Grimsby's parish church in 1586, when John Whitgift united two parishes.

name: Grimsby Town Hall
text: Your train passes Grimsby Town Hall, on the train's {side}, an Italianate building finished in 1863 on what had been open land called Six Acres Field. It is the town's fourth town hall: the first was built in the 13th century.

name: Grimsby Ice Factory
text: Your train passes near the Grimsby Ice Factory, on the train's {side}, built from 1898 to 1901 to make crushed ice for keeping fish fresh on the trawlers. At its height it made 1,200 tonnes of ice a day and was once the largest ice factory in the world; it closed in 1990.

name: Blundell Park
text: Your train passes near Blundell Park, on the train's {side}, home of Grimsby Town since 1899, although it is in Cleethorpes. Its record crowd, 31,651, came for an FA Cup tie against Wolverhampton Wanderers in 1937.

name: Bradford Cathedral
text: Your train passes near Bradford Cathedral, on the train's {side}, the church of St Peter, on a site used for Christian worship since the seventh century. It was Bradford's parish church for centuries and became a cathedral in 1919.

name: St Agatha's Chapel, Easby
text: Your train passes near St Agatha's Chapel, Easby, on the train's {side}, a private chapel built in 1881 for James Emerson of Easby Hall, with an octagonal mausoleum at its east end and a shingled spire.
